post.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF): Tailoring APIs for UI
post.subtitle: Mobile apps need less data than Desktop dashboards. Why serve them the same JSON? The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern solves this.
post.brief: A "one-size-fits-all" API causes bloated mobile payloads and underpowered desktop dashboards. The **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** pattern solves this by creating a dedicated API server for each client type — the mobile BFF reshapes data for small screens, the web BFF aggregates for dashboards.

content.markdown:
## Scenario context

A "one-size-fits-all" API causes bloated mobile payloads and underpowered desktop dashboards. The **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** pattern solves this by creating a dedicated API server for each client type — the mobile BFF reshapes data for small screens, the web BFF aggregates for dashboards.



```architecture
{
  "ok": true,
  "diagram": {
    "version": 1,
    "title": "Backend for Frontend (BFF) Pattern",
    "d…

This walkthrough focuses on **The One-Size-Fits-All API Problem**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- You have a mobile app and a web dashboard.
- The problem: - Mobile loads a user profile page.
- The generic /user/{id} endpoint returns 50 fields.

**Concepts in play:** api-gateway, load-balancing, event-driven-architecture, graph-traversal-algorithms

## Stage 1 — BFF Basics: One Backend Per Frontend

- A generic REST API returns the same response shape to every caller.
- That works for simple apps but breaks down when clients have radically different needs: - Mobile apps run on limited bandwidth and battery.
- They need compact, pre-computed responses.
- - Web dashboards need rich, aggregated data combining multiple domain objects.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Web dashboards need rich, aggregated data combining multiple domain objects.

## Stage 2 — One API Layer per Client Type

- The BFF pattern introduces a thin, client-specific server between each frontend and the shared microservices: Key properties: - Tight coupling by design: The Mobile BFF is owned by the mobile team.
- When the app screen changes, the BFF changes with it.
- - Data shaping: The BFF projects the microservice response to exactly what the client needs.
- - Protocol bridging: Microservices may speak gRPC internally.

*Applies **load-balancing** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
graph TD
    Mobile[Mobile App] --> MBFF[Mobile BFF]
    Web[Web Dashboard] --> WBFF[Web BFF]

    MBFF --> UserSvc[User Service]
    MBFF --> CartSvc[Cart Service]

    WBFF --> UserSvc
    WBFF --> CartSvc
    WBFF --> RecSvc[Recommendation Service]
    WBFF --> NotifSvc[Notification Service]
```

**Observable outcome:** - Protocol bridging: Microservices may speak gRPC internally.

## Stage 3 — Request Flow Through a BFF

- The request lifecycle from client to microservices flows through the BFF: Each step adds value: 1.
- Auth validation — the BFF verifies the token before hitting any upstream service.
- Parallel upstream calls — fan out to N services simultaneously to minimize latency.
- Response aggregation — merge the N responses into one JSON object.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Client Request] --> B{Which client?}
    B -->|Mobile| C[Mobile BFF]
    B -->|Web| D[Web BFF]
    C --> E[Auth Token Validation]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Parallel Upstream Calls]
    F --> G[User Service]
    F --> H[Cart Service]
    F --> I[Rec Service]
    G --> J[Response Aggregation]
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J --> K[Field Projection]
    K --> L[Client Response]
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant MB as Mobile App
  participant MBff as Mobile BFF
  participant WB as Web Dashboard
  participant WBff as Web BFF
  participant US as User Service
  participant CS as Cart Service
  participant RS as Rec Service
  MB->>MBff: GET /mobile/home/{userId}
  par parallel fetch
    MBff->>US: getUser(userId)
    US-->>MBff: firstName only
    MBff->>CS: getCart(userId)
    CS-->>MBff: itemCount only
  end
  MBff-->>MB: compact 8-field response
  WB->>WBff: GET /web/dashboard/{userId}
  par parallel fetch
    WBff->>US: getUser(userId)
    US-->>WBff: full profile
    WBff->>CS: getCart(userId)
    CS-->>WBff: full cart detail
    WBff->>RS: getTopRecs(userId)
    RS-->>WBff: 10 recommendations
  end
  WBff-->>WB: aggregated dashboard payload
```

**Observable outcome:** Response aggregation — merge the N responses into one JSON object.

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: What Lives Inside a BFF

- A BFF is not a full microservice.
- It is a lightweight orchestration layer.
- Typical responsibilities: A BFF should contain no business logic .
- If you find yourself writing pricing rules or fraud detection inside a BFF, that code belongs in a separate service.

*Applies **graph-traversal-algorithms** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** If you find yourself writing pricing rules or fraud detection inside a BFF, that code belongs in a separate service.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Parallel Aggregation: The Common BFF Pattern

- The most useful thing a BFF does is fan out requests and merge them: Three upstream calls run in parallel (~80 ms total instead of sequential ~240 ms).
- The client gets a single clean response in one round trip.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```python
# Mobile BFF: home screen endpoint
async def get_home_screen(user_id: str):
    user, cart, recommendations = await asyncio.gather(
        user_service.get(user_id),
        cart_service.get(user_id),
        rec_service.get_top5(user_id),
    )
    return {
        "name": user.first_name,
        "cart_count": len(cart.items),
        "recs": [r.title for r in recommendations],
    }
```

**Observable outcome:** The client gets a single clean response in one round trip.

## Stage 6 — Practical: Adding a New Mobile Screen

- Suppose you add a "notifications center" screen to the mobile app.
- The workflow with a BFF: Step 1 — Identify what the screen needs: - Unread notification count (from Notification Service) - Top 3 notification previews (from Notification Service) - User's preferred notification type (f…
- The web dashboard has its own endpoint for notifications with a different shape.
- This is the BFF promise: frontend-driven API changes stay contained to that frontend's BFF .

*Applies **load-balancing** to the decision above.*

```python
# Mobile BFF: notifications screen endpoint
async def get_notifications_screen(user_id: str):
    notifs, prefs = await asyncio.gather(
        notification_service.get_recent(user_id, limit=3),
        user_service.get_notification_prefs(user_id),
    )
    return {
        "unread_count": notifs.total_unread,
        "previews": [{"id": n.id, "text": n.text[:50]} for n in notifs.items],
        "sound_on": prefs.sound_enabled,
    }
```

**Observable outcome:** This is the BFF promise: frontend-driven API changes stay contained to that frontend's BFF .

## End-to-end outcome

You have a mobile app and a web dashboard.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Trade-offs, Failure Modes & Decision Guide

- **Detection:** BFF is not always the right answer: Code duplication risk: If mobile and web BFFs share 80% of logic, refactor the common parts into shared service clients — not into both BFFs.
- **User or operator impact:** BFF is not always the right answer: Code duplication risk: If mobile and web BFFs share 80% of logic, refactor the common parts into shared service clients — not into both BFFs.
